name: Leader Election Patterns
tagline: Choosing one cluster coordinator via majority quorum while protecting external storage with monotonic epoch fencing.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of leader election—from why split-brain corrupts state to how Raft quorums, pre-vote, and fencing tokens keep distributed clusters safe.

spark.summary: Leader election chooses one coordinator to sequence updates across a cluster while a majority confirms them. It helps replicas maintain one consistent history. The trade-off: failover delays writes and external systems need fencing.
spark.keyTakeaway: A leader coordinates changes. A majority decides. Fencing protects external state when old leaders wake back up.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Leader election** coordinates state changes across distributed nodes by appointing a single coordinator to sequence writes.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Leader Election State Machine (Follower / Candidate / Leader) (FOLLOWER -> CANDIDATE -> LEADER); How Monotonic Fencing Stops a Zombie Leader (Old Leader (T105) -> Quorum (B, C) -> New Leader (T106) -> Fenced Storage); 3-Node Raft Election & Replication Topology (Node A (Leader) -> Node B (Follower) -> Node C (Follower)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choosing between consensus-backed leadership, wall-clock leases, and leaderless coordination trades latency for safety. A follower's acknowledgment confirms durable log storage (`fsync`), not execution.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore concrete distributed consensus problems, split-brain postmortems, and fencing architectures.

learningJourney.title: What is Leader Election
learningJourney.explanation:
**Leader election** coordinates state changes across distributed nodes by appointing a single coordinator to sequence writes. If two nodes both think they are in charge, they accept conflicting updates—a failure called **split-brain**.

Consensus protocols like **Raft** prevent conflicting leaders using a majority of voting nodes (**quorum**): $Q \ge \lfloor N / 2 \rfloor + 1$. Because any two majorities of $N = 2F + 1$ nodes overlap by at least one voter, at most one leader can be elected in any given **term** (epoch).

sectionDiagram.title: Leader Election State Machine (Follower / Candidate / Leader)
sectionDiagram.summary: Randomized election timeouts (150–300 ms) break ties so one candidate wins quorum instead of looping on split votes.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Quorum Election & Monotonic Fencing
learningJourney.explanation:
A cluster cannot tell whether a silent leader crashed or is paused by a stop-the-world GC or asymmetric network partition. Even after a majority partition elects a new leader in Term 106, the isolated old leader (Term 105) may wake up and flush a stale write to external storage.

**Monotonic epoch fencing** solves this: every newly elected leader mints an incrementing epoch token, and downstream storage rejects any write carrying a token lower than the highest accepted watermark.

sectionDiagram.title: How Monotonic Fencing Stops a Zombie Leader
sectionDiagram.summary: Quorum prevents two leaders in the same term; storage-side fencing prevents an old-term zombie from corrupting state.

ideas.title: Odd Voter Counts (2F + 1)
ideas.description: A 4-node cluster still needs 3 votes for quorum—tolerating only 1 failure, identical to 3 nodes, while adding replication overhead.

ideas.title: Pre-Vote Phase
ideas.description: Before incrementing its term, a partitioned node checks if a majority would vote for it, preventing isolated nodes from disrupting a healthy leader on reconnect.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Quorum Election & Monotonic Fencing under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Leader Election is used (and where to avoid it)
learningJourney.explanation: Use leader election when a cluster needs a single writer to serialize metadata, partition ownership, or state machine logs.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Consensus Metadata & Control Planes
benefits: etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka KRaft controller, and Consul elect one leader for linearizable cluster state.
costs: All control-plane writes route through one leader, capping write QPS.

benefits: Patroni/etcd automates primary promotion on crash while fencing the old primary.
costs: Failover window (typically 5–30 s) pauses writes during election.

benefits: L4/L7 load balancers or leaderless gossip/CRDTs scale horizontally without a single bottleneck.
costs: Cannot enforce strict total write ordering without a coordinator.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Leaders replicate logs and enforce fencing
learningJourney.explanation: A follower's acknowledgment confirms durable log storage (`fsync`), not execution. Replicas apply entries to their state machine only after the leader advances `commitIndex`. For external side effects, the storage layer enforces atomic monotonic token checks.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Consensus Quorum vs. Lease Timeouts vs. Leaderless
learningJourney.explanation: Choosing between consensus-backed leadership, wall-clock leases, and leaderless coordination trades latency for safety.

benefits: Linearizable safety across partitions; immune to NTP clock skew.
costs: Quorum RTT + disk fsync limits raw write throughput.

benefits: Simpler external integration with lower coordination overhead.
costs: Vulnerable to NTP jumps and JVM/Go GC pauses exceeding lease TTL.

benefits: High write availability across partitions with no failover pause.
costs: Requires client conflict resolution (LWW, vector clocks, or CRDTs).

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: 3-Node Consensus Quorum + Fenced Storage
learningJourney.explanation: In production control planes, an odd-sized Raft quorum (3 or 5 nodes across availability zones) sequences terms and replicates the write-ahead log, while downstream databases enforce the term/revision watermark.

sectionDiagram.title: 3-Node Raft Election & Replication Topology

cards.label: 1. Quorum (2 of 3)
cards.detail: Leader A + Follower B form a majority; Node C can be down or partitioned without stalling writes.

cards.label: 2. Pre-Vote Guard
cards.detail: Reconnecting Node C runs Pre-Vote before bumping Term so it cannot depose healthy Leader A.

cards.label: 3. Fenced Downstream
cards.detail: All external writes carry Term 106; storage rejects any delayed Term <= 105 request.

sectionDiagram.summary: Odd-sized quorums (3 or 5) maximize fault tolerance per node while pre-vote and fencing eliminate partition-heal storms.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should consensus clusters deploy 3 or 5 voting nodes rather than 4?

options.text: 4-node clusters cannot run the Raft algorithm
options.feedback: Raft works with any N, but even N wastes a node's fault tolerance.

options.text: Both 4-node and 3-node clusters tolerate at most 1 node failure (quorum=3 vs 2), so the 4th node adds replication cost with zero extra fault tolerance
options.feedback: Correct: floor(4/2)+1 = 3, meaning 4 nodes can only lose 1 node before losing quorum—the same as 3 nodes.

options.text: 4-node clusters double write latency compared to 5-node clusters
options.feedback: Quorum size is 3 in both 4- and 5-node clusters, but 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures instead of 1.
